keyTerms.definition: z in R^V, one real number per vocabulary token.
Turns logits into probabilities: p_i = exp(z_i / T) / sum_j exp(z_j / T).
Sharpens toward argmax as T approaches 0; flattens toward uniform as T grows.
O(n^2 d) per layer; the (n, n) score matrix dominates long contexts.

recall.answer: At T = 1 it is plain softmax. As T approaches 0 the distribution sharpens toward the argmax. As T grows it flattens toward uniform. Every sampling decision in U01 is an operation on this vector.
recall.question: What does the temperature knob do?

keyTerms.definition: Shells 0-6: from one fixed logit vector to a controllable sampler.
Greedy choice; the T -> 0 limit puts probability 1 on it.
Divide by T, exponentiate, normalize, sample; the shell-3 rule.

recall.answer: Shell 0 asks how one logit vector becomes controllable choices. Shells 1-3 build the toy ([1.0, 2.0, 3.0]) and the divide-exponentiate-normalize-sample rule. Shells 4-6 derive the T -> 0 limit, check sums to 1, and predict flattening at T = 3.

keyTerms.definition: Answered in C04 via variance of the dot product.
Changes per-token cost from quadratic to linear in n; answered in C06.

recall.answer: Why attention divides by sqrt(d_k) (C04), how the KV cache changes per-token cost (C06), and when retrieval beats a bigger model (C12 via the selection table).
recall.question: What does the dependency list resolve and where?

keyTerms.definition: The pair (O_i, I_j) between components; what format crosses each boundary.
Components (model, retriever, tools, checks) joined by interfaces; looks things up, computes, checks.
System accuracy follows pipeline logic (retriever AND model-use), not a product of accuracies.

recall.answer: A model is a function from tokens to tokens. A system is components joined by interfaces. In the toy, the model alone scores 3/10; the system scores 8/10 at 4 times the token cost.
recall.question: What distinguishes a model from a system?

recall.answer: Break the testable-alone assumption: a retriever returning plausible but wrong chunks that the model trusts drops the system to 2/10, worse than the model alone. A same-model retriever is not a system.
recall.question: When is the system worse than the model?

keyTerms.definition: g_i: O_i -> {pass, fail}; the whole point of the split.
A wrong final answer with subtask 2 passed localizes the fault to subtask 1 or the gate.
The SRC-04 example: write copy, then translate, with a style check between.

recall.answer: Cut the task where a check can verify the cut. Each subtask gets an input contract, an output contract, and a test. Without the gate the split is decoration.
recall.question: Where do you cut a task?

recall.answer: Break the checkable-seam assumption: a gate that is the same model agreeing with its own bad draft fails silently. Splitting translation into one subtask per sentence is over-decomposition.
recall.question: What breaks decomposition?

keyTerms.definition: sqrt(m(1-m)/n) for a rate; the 8/10 vs 7/10 gap sits inside the noise at n = 10.
The specification: if you cannot say what good looks like on 50 examples, you cannot build toward it.
Eval items must represent the deployment distribution, or every number lies.

recall.answer: The standard error of 8/10 at n = 10 is 0.13, so the 0.1 gap is noise. Neither ships on this evidence; grow the eval first.
recall.question: Two systems score 8/10 and 7/10. Which ships?

recall.answer: Break representativeness: an easy-only eval scores 0.95 while production is 0.5. An eval leaking into training measures memory, not ability.
recall.question: What breaks an eval?

keyTerms.definition: A weighted vote: queries ask, keys label, values message; weights come from the softmax.
Restores unit variance to dot products so large d_k does not kill gradients.
Forgetting it lets token 5 read token 6 in training; great loss, garbage generation.

recall.answer: Each token asks a question (query), every token posts a label (key) and a message (value). The token listens most to messages whose labels match its question.
recall.question: How does attention read?

recall.answer: Break the causal mask and training sees the future. Identical keys make the weights uniform and the vote meaningless.
recall.question: What breaks attention?

keyTerms.definition: Rolls a weighted die over the reshaped distribution.
Throws away all but the k best faces of the die.
H(T) rises with T: 0.23 nats at 0.2, 0.83 at 1, 1.06 at 3 for the toy logits.

recall.answer: Greedy takes the max, temperature sampling rolls a weighted die, top-k keeps the k best faces, top-p adds faces until mass reaches p. At T = 1 on logits [1,2,3], token 1 appears about 9 times in 100.
recall.question: What are the four decoding controls?

recall.answer: Break calibration: 0.99 on a wrong token makes temperature useless; low T repeats the error confidently. Tied logits make the winner a tie-break artifact.
recall.question: What breaks decoding controls?

keyTerms.definition: Shape (L, 2, n, d); about 0.5 MB per token at L = 32, d = 4096, fp16.
Each new token costs O(n d) attention over the cache, not O(n^2 d).
Mid-context evidence gets ignored; position matters for retrieval use.

recall.answer: The context window is short-term memory; the KV cache is the filing cabinet making rereading cheap. Context engineering decides what earns a slot: instructions, evidence, history, tool results.
recall.question: What is context engineering?

recall.answer: Break relevance: 100k tokens of near-duplicate docs make answers worse than the top 5 chunks. Lost-in-the-middle placement gets evidence ignored.
recall.question: What breaks long context?

keyTerms.definition: A JSON schema with typed fields; turns prose into data.
The handshake: downstream can rely on the shape only if it runs.
You promise a shape, the model promises to fill it.

recall.answer: Parse-then-validate: json.loads(o), then check field types and required keys, O(size of o). The schema check is a cheap gate converting silent data corruption into a loud error.
recall.question: How does validation work?

recall.answer: Break coverage: demanding an unknowable field (invoice_id) makes the model hallucinate it; the contract creates the lie. Top-level-only validation misses nested breakage.
recall.question: What breaks structured I/O?

keyTerms.definition: m_i = 1 if i in A else 0; tokens 4 and 5 are masked in the toy.
Conditioning the categorical on {token in A} gives exactly the masked softmax.
Allowing any string for date yields yesterday: valid JSON, useless data.

recall.answer: Mask tokens 4 and 5 (they would break the JSON), keep allowed logits [2.0, 1.5, 1.0], renormalize. Prevention during sampling beats validation after the fact.
recall.question: How do you prevent bad JSON during sampling?

recall.answer: Break the grammar: a permissive date schema emits yesterday. A regex permitting {} makes the sampler emit it with high probability.
recall.question: What breaks constrained decoding?

keyTerms.definition: Teaches how the world talks; capabilities come mostly from its scale.
Minimizes -log P(response | prompt) on demonstrations: pure imitation.
Annotators rewarding you are so right teaches flattery instead of help.

recall.answer: Pretraining teaches how the world talks; post-training teaches behavior: follow instructions, refuse harm, match preferences. Capabilities come from pretraining scale, behavior from post-training.
recall.question: What do pretraining and post-training each teach?

recall.answer: Break the values assumption: sycophancy-rewarding annotators teach flattery. Post-training a must-answer topic into refusal breaks the task.
recall.question: What breaks post-training?

keyTerms.definition: Best-of-k needs only one good sample; the picker over k tries.
More samples, longer chains, more search; all spend inference tokens.

recall.answer: pass@k follows from independence. Majority vote needs p > 0.5 per sample to help. A verifier needs only one good sample among k. All assume independence and checkable success.
recall.question: What does each test-time currency assume?

recall.answer: Break independence: the same systematic mistake 8 times keeps pass@8 at 0.3. With no verifier and p < 0.5, majority vote amplifies the wrong answer.
recall.question: What breaks test-time scaling?

keyTerms.definition: The scoreboard: 0.62 at 1x cost in the toy; every component must beat it per dollar.
Without it, every new component is a story, not a result.
Incremental comparison in reverse: add components, do not subtract.

recall.answer: Keep component i if (b_i - b_0) / (c_i - c_0) clears the bar. Simple first also ships fastest, buying the eval data later components need.
recall.question: When is a component kept?

recall.answer: Break the eval: a baseline overfit to 20 items makes every addition fail against a lucky bar. A 0.1 baseline makes anything look like a breakthrough; the bar must be honest.
recall.question: What breaks the baseline discipline?

keyTerms.definition: Ask: is the path known? Is knowledge in weights or docs? Is success checkable?
Maps property combinations to the cheapest satisfying pattern; not a formula.
Answer questions over 10k docs; the compound pattern for doc-knowledge tasks.

recall.answer: (a) tickets by topic: single call. (b) draft then translate: prompt chaining workflow. (c) questions over 10k docs: RAG compound system. Fancy patterns on simple tasks are cost without gain.
recall.question: How do the four toy tasks map to architectures?

recall.answer: Break stability: a known-path task drifting open-ended after launch breaks the workflow. A 10ms latency budget makes the correct agent too slow; the table must include latency.
recall.question: What breaks the architecture choice?
